node.date_label: 1995: Homo sacer: Il potere sovrano e la nuda vita (Italian original) · 1998: Homo Sacer: Sovereign Power and Bare Life (Daniel Heller-Roazen English translation) · 2003: Stato di eccezione (Italian original) · 2009: What Is an Apparatus? and Other Essays (David Kishik and Stefan Pedatella English translation)
node.description: A philosopher of sovereignty, law and forms of life whose Homo sacer project uses historical paradigms to examine political structures. In his own account, the state of exception connects law with anomy; he distinguishes this paradigmatic method from a comprehensive historical survey.

people_update.label: Giorgio Agamben
people_update.identity_note: Giorgio Agamben, born 1942, identified through the European Graduate School biography’s concordant Homo sacer (1995) and Stato di eccezione (2003), and the named 2004 Raulff interview about those works. New curated identity giorgio_agamben; no authority ID guessed, automatic crosswalk or namesake merger.

proposed_edges.relationship: Uses the state of exception as a paradigm for examining the relation of law, anomy and governmental power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own interview pp. 609–612 read. The emergency-to-normal-government thesis is attributed to Agamben; this is a philosophical paradigm rather than independent verification of an encompassing history of states.

proposed_edges.relationship: Agamben explicitly invokes Foucault’s panopticon and archaeology as resources for his paradigmatic method.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own interview pp. 610 and 613 read. Acknowledged methodological resource, not an assertion that Foucault endorsed Agamben or that their projects coincide.

new_sources.title: Ulrich Raulff, An Interview with Giorgio Agamben, German Law Journal 5.5 (2004): 609–614; Morag Goodwin translation

verification.note: Complete interview pp. 609–614 including editorial notes read. Conversation Rome 4 March 2004; German Süddeutsche Zeitung publication 6 April; English translation Morag Goodwin. Agamben explicitly distinguishes paradigmatic method from being a historian and names Foucault’s panopticon/archaeology as resources. Editor notes are distinct from answers. Incidental 1968 Collège course and 1934 Nuremberg-law dates are erroneous and not adopted; policy/historical generalizations are attributed, not independently established. Books unread.
